title: The Global South: the 21st century’s great utopia
gist: Stephen Kotkin argues the 'Global South' is a historically hollow, incoherent category that mainly functions as an instrument of Chinese soft power and UN-reform utopianism; the US is not in structural decline (still ~25% of global GDP), and the realistic path to preserving a workable rules-based order is 'middle-power horizontalism' — regional and cross-regional cooperation among countries like Japan, India, Australia and the Nordics — linked to a rebalanced (not absent) US leadership.

themes.theme: Stubb's 'Triangle of Power' and why its UN-reform plan is unworkable

insights.claim: Finnish President Alexander Stubb's 2026 book 'The Triangle of Power' divides the world into a 'Global West' (North America, EU, UK, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Israel, Australia, New Zealand — shared democratic institutions), a 'Global East' (China, Russia, Iran, Belarus, North Korea — shared illiberal institutions), and a residual 'Global South' spanning countries from Argentina to Afghanistan with no shared institutions or values.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Provides the specific three-bloc taxonomy Kotkin is arguing against — a useful reference framework for classifying countries in geopolitical/allocation models, even though Kotkin ultimately rejects its 'Global South' category as incoherent.
insights.quote: One corner encompasses the ‘Global West’, including North America, the European Union and the United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan, Israel, Australia and New Zealand, a grouping founded upon shared values and institutions
insights.locator: Opening section on Alexander Stubb's book

insights.claim: Stubb proposes restructuring the UN by adding five new permanent Security Council seats for Africa, Asia and Latin America, abolishing Security Council vetoes, and suspending voting rights for members that violate the UN Charter (e.g., by launching wars of aggression, as Russia did against Ukraine).
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Specifies the concrete UN reform proposal on the table from a sitting G7-adjacent head of state, useful for tracking any future momentum (or lack thereof) behind Security Council reform.
insights.quote: an expansion of the Security Council with five new permanent seats for Africa, Asia and Latin America, abolition of Security Council vetoes, and temporary suspensions of voting rights for members
insights.locator: Paragraph on Stubb's mechanism via a structurally remade UN

insights.claim: Kotkin argues Stubb's UN Charter reform is not practically achievable because Article 109 requires a General Conference to review the Charter, but this in turn requires consent from all five permanent Security Council members (US, UK, France, China, Russia) — meaning China and Russia would have to agree to reforms designed to curb states like themselves.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A concrete, high-conviction reason to discount near-term UN Security Council reform as a realistic policy path — relevant to any thesis premised on UN institutional overhaul.
insights.quote: Article 109 does provide for a General Conference to review and amend the Charter, but that would require consent from all five permanent Security Council members: the US, UK, France, China and Russia.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'The Finnish President does not offer a persuasive sense'

insights.claim: Kotkin's central thesis is that the notion of a new world order shaped by the Global South is a chimera — a 21st-century utopia in the tradition of Thomas More, revealing a paucity of workable alternatives rather than a coherent path forward.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: The essay's overarching claim — investors and policymakers treating 'Global South' as a coherent bloc with unified interests (for trade, voting, or investment allocation purposes) are working from a flawed premise per Kotkin.
insights.quote: President Stubb’s version is the Global West’s rules-based order being preserved by coalition with the Global South. In truth, this indicates a paucity of workable options
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'It might be tempting to ridicule this wager'

themes.theme: The 'Third World' to 'Global South' lineage: an instrumental, not descriptive, term

insights.claim: The term 'Third World' originated in a 1952 French newspaper article by demographer Alfred Sauvy, who explicitly modeled it on the Abbé Sieyès' 1789 pamphlet describing France's Third Estate ('What is the Third Estate? Everything...What does it ask? To become something').
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Traces the intellectual lineage of a term still used casually in geopolitical/investment discourse today, showing it was coined as a political grievance-mobilisation device rather than an economic classification.
insights.quote: ‘What is the Third Estate? Everything. What has it been hitherto in the political order? Nothing. What does it ask? To become something.’
insights.locator: Section 'From the Third World to the Global South'

insights.claim: The term 'Global South' is generally attributed to American New Left activist Carl Oglesby, who used it in 1969 during the Vietnam War era to describe the 'North's dominance over the global south,' but it saw little use until 1980, when World Bank president Robert McNamara invited former West German Chancellor Willy Brandt to chair an international development commission.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Establishes the term's origin in 1960s-70s New Left activism rather than economic or demographic analysis, reinforcing Kotkin's argument that it is a political construct.
insights.quote: decried the ‘North’s dominance over the global south’
insights.locator: Section 'From the Third World to the Global South'

insights.claim: Willy Brandt's 1980 commission report, 'North-South: a Program for Survival,' called for a massive transfer of resources from a wealthy 'North' to a poorer 'South' as a matter of mutual interest, but none of its recommendations were ever implemented, and international development aid more broadly generally failed to bring about development.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A concrete historical case where a high-profile, elite-endorsed redistribution framework produced zero policy follow-through — relevant precedent for skepticism toward current 'Global South'-framed redistribution or reparations proposals.
insights.quote: None of the Brandt Report’s recommendations were implemented. In fact, international development aid, before and after the report, generally failed to bring about development.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'None of the Brandt Report's recommendations'

insights.claim: Kotkin's causal claim: it was markets — trade, investment, and technology transfer, enabled by US-provided security, finance and trading architecture — not aid programs, that created a global middle class of unprecedented size and reduced poverty for countries that did not need navies or great-power status to participate.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A high-conviction, contrarian-to-consensus causal claim (markets beat aid) directly relevant to development-economics and emerging-market investment theses, and to the broader debate over aid effectiveness.
insights.quote: Instead, markets – with trade, investment, technology transfer – created a global middle class unprecedented in size, and reduced poverty, unlike most poverty programmes.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'None of the Brandt Report's recommendations'

insights.claim: Ironically, while Brandt's report called for redistribution abroad, Sweden's own Social Democrats began rolling back the domestic welfare state from around 1970 onward, eventually enacting pension reform (which enabled the birth of Sweden's venture capital industry) and allowing privatisation in healthcare and schools; Kotkin notes 'this is where the UK sits today.'
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Draws a direct historical-parallel warning: Sweden's fiscal retrenchment eventually catalyzed its VC industry, offered as an implicit model/warning for the UK's current fiscal trajectory.
insights.quote: Crucially, the government instituted pension reform (which would later enable the birth of their venture capital industry), and even allowed privatisation in healthcare and school systems to foster competition.
insights.locator: Paragraphs on Sweden's welfare-state rollback

insights.claim: Several former 'Third World' countries have since joined the West (South Korea, Taiwan) or risen to upper-middle income (Botswana, Mauritius, Colombia, Peru, Costa Rica, Indonesia, China) or high income (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Singapore) — a 'graduation dilemma' some Third World advocates (particularly in Brazil) have lamented because it undermines the political basis for continued aid.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A striking, underappreciated point: development success stories create an incentive problem for the aid/grievance advocacy industry, which several countries citing 'Global South' status have flagged as a concern.
insights.quote: some Third World advocates (particularly in Brazil) lamented a ‘graduation dilemma’ that undermined the basis for aid
insights.locator: Paragraph on countries joining the West or rising income tiers

insights.claim: Kotkin argues that romanticized accounts of pre-Western 'world systems' — William Dalrymple's Indosphere 'Golden Road,' Janet Abu-Lughod's Mongol-era trading circuits, and Ayşe Zarakol's 'Chinggisid world order' — impute a coherence and capacity to the pre-modern past that the historical record does not support, driven by a longing for a non-Western-dominated world.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A methodological caution against treating currently fashionable 'multipolar pre-Western order' scholarship as evidence that a non-Western-led global system is historically viable or desirable.
insights.quote: The longing for a time when the world was not Western-dominated, especially not US-dominated, has led some scholars to invent a past that aligns with their hopes for the future
insights.locator: Section 'Pre-Western World Systems?'

insights.claim: Estimates of deaths caused by the 'Pax Mongolica' — through executions, infanticide, burnings and irrigation destruction — approach 29 million, more than Stalin's death toll and exceeded only by Mao's, in the same geographies.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A stark data point undercutting nostalgic framings of Mongol-era 'world order' as a benign or peaceful precedent for a post-Western future.
insights.quote: estimates of deaths from the ‘Pax Mongolica’ – by executions, infanticide, burnings, irrigation destruction – approach 29 million, more than Stalin and topped only by Mao, in the same geographies
insights.locator: Paragraph on Mongol political order

insights.claim: Kotkin concludes that no equitable, fundamentally peaceful and mostly law-based pre-European order exists in the historical record that could serve as an adaptable model for a post-Western future.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts the premise that a 'return' to pre-Western multipolarity would be more just or stable than the current US-led order.
insights.quote: An equitable, fundamentally peaceful and mostly law-based pre-European order, to serve as an adaptable model for the future, is hard to find in the past.
insights.locator: End of section on Mongol political order

themes.theme: Western dominance and decline were self-inflicted, and the US is not in decline

insights.claim: Europe's population grew from around 100 million to over 400 million in the 19th century; its states, at roughly 20 in number after consolidating from about 500 four centuries earlier, controlled 84% of world territory in 1900 despite occupying only 8% of the Earth's land mass, and its share of global GDP peaked at around 46%.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of pre-WWI European global dominance as the baseline against which to measure its subsequent decline.
insights.quote: European states and monarchs laid claim to 84 per cent of the world’s territory at that time.
insights.locator: Section 'Western Civilisation: Murder or Suicide?'

insights.claim: Europe's dominance ended through self-inflicted 'fratricide' — the US rescued Western Europe from defeat by Central Europe in WWI, and the US and USSR combined to rescue it in WWII — after which decolonisation produced almost half of the world's present-day nation-states within 30 years of 1945.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Frames the collapse of European global primacy as caused by Europe's own internal wars rather than external conquest — relevant historical context for assessing whether current Western decline narratives are similarly self-inflicted (e.g., internal political dysfunction vs. external rival strength).
insights.quote: Europe had helped shift the balance of power against itself by aggression and overreach.
insights.locator: Section 'Western Civilisation: Murder or Suicide?'

insights.claim: Europe (including the UK) has fallen from roughly one-third of global GDP in the 1960s and 30% in 1992 to about 17% as of 2025.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Concrete, time-stamped GDP-share data tracking Europe's relative economic decline over six decades — a benchmark figure for assessing European weight in global economic/political forecasting.
insights.quote: Europe (including the UK) has fallen back to some 17 per cent (as of 2025).
insights.locator: Section 'Western Civilisation: Murder or Suicide?'

insights.claim: Kotkin's central contrarian claim: the United States is not in decline — it still accounts for a quarter of global GDP, the same proportion as in 1880, alongside the world's most dynamic economy and strong (if stressed) institutions.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Directly counters the dominant 'US in terminal decline' narrative with a specific, checkable GDP-share statistic — a key reference point for any US-decline vs. US-resilience investment or geopolitical thesis.
insights.quote: the United States is not in decline: it continues to account for a quarter of global GDP, the same proportion as in 1880, with the world’s most dynamic economy, strong if stressed institutions, and a robust self-organised society
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'But the United States is not in decline'

insights.claim: China's regime paradoxically still needs the US-led open global system, both to absorb its exports (which deindustrialises its trade competitors) and for technology leakage, even as the CCP works to sap US power while publicly calling for 'stabilisation' of relations that in practice means blocking US responses to China's economic pressure.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A structural dependency claim useful for assessing the limits of Chinese decoupling rhetoric — China's own growth model still relies on access to Western-anchored markets even as it pressures those same markets diplomatically.
insights.quote: Paradoxically, China’s regime continues to need the US-led open global system, if only to absorb its exports (and deindustrialise its competitors) and for tech leakage.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'China is an extraordinary civilisation'

themes.theme: China's instrumental use of 'Global South' framing

insights.claim: China positions itself simultaneously in the illiberal 'Global East' (alongside Russia, Iran, Belarus, North Korea) and claims membership of the 'Global South' — a strategic dual-positioning that echoes its Cold War-era claim to Third World solidarity while competing with the USSR for Second World primacy.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Highlights a specific strategic ambiguity China exploits in international forums — claiming both great-power and developing-country status simultaneously — relevant for interpreting China's positioning in trade and climate negotiations.
insights.quote: China claims also to be in the Global South (Third World), a familiar problem from the time when China competed with the USSR for primacy in the Second World on the basis of claiming to be in the Third.
insights.locator: Second paragraph, on Stubb's triangle

insights.claim: The G77 bloc at the UN General Assembly, founded in 1964, has grown to 134 members and often votes as a bloc; China uses this leverage to build symbolic support for its positions, including its false interpretation of UN General Assembly Resolution 2758 (1971) as having resolved Taiwan's sovereignty, when in fact it only transferred the UN China seat to the PRC.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable legal/diplomatic misrepresentation (Resolution 2758) that China leverages via the G77 bloc — directly relevant to assessing legal-narrative risk around Taiwan's international status.
insights.quote: China further manipulates the G77 to constrict UN spending on human rights (in the sense of civil liberties), while redefining the concept to its opposite (statism).
insights.locator: Paragraph on the G77's role

insights.claim: China has launched a succession of institution-building initiatives to assert global leadership: the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (2001), Belt and Road Initiative (2013), Global Development Initiative (2021), Global Security Initiative (2022), Global Civilisation Initiative (2023), and Global Governance Initiative (2025).
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A concrete, chronological timeline of China's parallel-institution strategy — useful as a tracking checklist for China's expanding soft-power/institutional footprint versus existing multilateral bodies.
insights.quote: Now China’s ambitions are grander still, as reflected in the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (2001), Belt and Road Initiative (2013), Global Development Initiative (2021), Global Security Initiative (2022)
insights.locator: End of section 'Non-Aligned Myths'

insights.claim: China markets its technology, tech standards and payment systems as a 'Global South-friendly' alternative to US systems, but Kotkin argues this in practice locks in CCP surveillance capabilities, data capture and leverage over adopting countries rather than offering genuine sovereignty.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A direct warning for countries or investors evaluating adoption of Chinese tech/payment infrastructure (e.g., surveillance systems, digital payment rails) marketed as sovereignty-friendly alternatives to Western systems.
insights.quote: China markets its technology, tech standards and payment systems as a Global-South friendly alternative to the US, rather than as a lock-in of the CCP’s surveillance capabilities, data capture and leverage.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'China is an extraordinary civilisation'

insights.claim: Developing countries are broadly wary of China, viewing it as both an indispensable economic partner and a security threat, and some Chinese economic policies are seen as actively deindustrialising developing-country competitors.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A relevant framing for emerging-market industrial-policy and 'de-risking' theses — China is simultaneously courted and feared by the very countries it claims to represent as 'Global South' partner.
insights.quote: developing countries tend to be wary of China, which many have viewed as an indispensable economic partner but also a security threat.
insights.locator: Section 'Neither South nor Global'

themes.theme: Bandung (1955) and the myth of an effective non-aligned bloc

insights.claim: The 1955 Bandung Conference drew roughly 2,000 attendees from 29 Asian/African states, deliberately excluded apartheid South Africa and the USSR, and saw the US decline to send executive-branch officials after Secretary of State John Foster Dulles refused to authorise attendance.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Establishes Bandung as the historical origin point often invoked as precedent for a unified 'Global South' voice, setting up Kotkin's argument that it never produced durable institutions.
insights.quote: All told, nearly 2,000 attendees, including 300 delegates and more than 650 foreign journalists, as well as staff, advisors and guests, jammed a newly reconstructed auditorium
insights.locator: Section 'Non-Aligned Myths'

insights.claim: Bandung's core failure, per Kotkin, is that it produced only a communiqué rather than a multilateral trading order, security architecture, or development bank; Nehru personally opposed forming any permanent organisation from the conference.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Explains structurally why Bandung-style solidarity conferences historically fail to translate into durable institutions with actual economic or security leverage.
insights.quote: Bandung’s achievement was also its failure: it was a conference, not a multilateral trading order combined with a security architecture, a development bank, a well-funded global health organisation, or even a membership club.
insights.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Decolonisation as celebrated at Bandung'

insights.claim: The Non-Aligned Movement, whose first summit convened in Belgrade in 1961, was not a follow-up to Bandung but its rival, and it never coalesced effectively because member interests diverged and most states still needed alignment with the US for security, investment and technology transfer.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Corrects a common historical misconception (NAM as Bandung's heir) and reinforces the broader thesis that 'non-alignment' has never been a practically viable strategy given real dependence on great-power ties.
insights.quote: Myths arose that Ghana’s Nkrumah and Yugoslavia’s Josip Briz Tito, among others, had attended the earlier Bandung. In fact, the Non-Aligned Movement was not Bandung’s follow-up but its rival.
insights.locator: Paragraph on the 1961 Belgrade conference

insights.claim: Subsequent Non-Aligned Movement summits were hosted by increasingly authoritarian states — Iran (2012), Venezuela (2016), Azerbaijan (2019), Uganda (2024), with Uzbekistan next in line — undermining its claim to represent a genuine 'voice of the voiceless.'
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Documents the movement's drift toward authoritarian host-state capture, further evidence against treating NAM-style forums as neutral or democratic representative bodies.
insights.quote: Subsequent NAM conferences took place in Islamist Tehran (2012), Nicolás Maduro’s Venezuela (2016), Azerbaijan’s hereditary dictatorship (2019) and authoritarian Uganda (2024). Dictatorial Uzbekistan hopes to host the next gathering.
insights.locator: Paragraph on subsequent NAM conferences

themes.theme: Middle-power horizontalism as the realistic path forward

insights.claim: Kotkin's proposed alternative to both 'Global South' utopianism and non-alignment is 'middle-power horizontalism' — deepening regional and cross-regional cooperation among countries like Japan, France, India, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, Mexico, the UAE, Singapore, Finland and Sweden, linked to (not replacing) a successfully rebalanced US leadership.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: The essay's central actionable framework: rather than betting on 'Global South' coalitions or UN reform, investors and policymakers should track deepening middle-power bilateral/regional pacts as the real vector of global-order stability.
insights.quote: if there is a solution to the unjust and unstable global order, it could turn out to be what I dub middle-power horizontalism.
insights.locator: Section 'A Renewed Global West with Middle-Power Activism?'

insights.claim: Examples of middle-power horizontalism already underway include India's economic agreements with Gulf states plus security/economic cooperation with Israel and Vietnam; Australia's defence treaty and economic partnership with Japan plus a defence pact and free trade agreement with the EU; and the Joint Expeditionary Force linking the five Nordic countries, three Baltic states, the Netherlands and the UK.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A concrete, trackable list of real-world alliance and trade structures already exemplifying the middle-power horizontalism thesis — a watchlist for cross-regional security/trade deal flow.
insights.quote: A group of NATO members have formed the Joint Expeditionary Force partnership consisting of the five Nordics, three Baltics, Netherlands and the UK. This is middle-power horizontalism.
insights.locator: Paragraph on deepening cross-regional lattice work

insights.claim: Kotkin warns that the global economic and security commons cannot survive without committed, competent US leadership, pointing to existing strains in the South China Sea, Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz, and flagging the Arctic Ocean, Baltic Sea, Strait of Malacca, Luzon Strait, La Pérouse Strait and Taiwan Strait as further potential freedom-of-navigation flashpoints.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: Gives an explicit, named watchlist of maritime chokepoints where reduced US leadership could translate into freedom-of-navigation disruption — directly relevant to shipping, energy and insurance risk assessment.
insights.quote: The belief that our global ‘operating system’ could survive without committed and competent US leadership is comforting to some but belied by the examples of the South China Sea, the Red Sea and now the Strait of Hormuz
insights.locator: Paragraph on none of these initiatives guaranteeing survival of the commons

insights.claim: Kotkin frames three fundamental, interacting questions as decisive for the future world order: whether the US successfully rebalances its global commitments and fixes domestic challenges; whether the EU can get unstuck from being unable to advance to full federation or retreat; and whether Chinese Communist Party rule survives its fear of and alienation from its own people absent any political-reform equilibrium for communist systems.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A concise top-level watchlist of the three variables Kotkin considers actually decisive for global order — a useful macro/geopolitical framework for structuring longer-horizon scenario analysis.
insights.quote: First, will the United States successfully rebalance its commitments and position globally, and put its own house in order, attending to its domestic challenges?
insights.locator: Paragraph on three fundamental questions of global trendlines

insights.claim: Kotkin explicitly rejects the BRICS as a viable alternative economic and financial architecture, noting they have failed to introduce one and that two of the bloc's newer members are at war with each other.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: A direct, specific rebuttal of BRICS-as-alternative-order narratives, relevant to assessing de-dollarisation and BRICS-institutional-alternative investment theses.
insights.quote: a paean to the BRICS, which have failed to introduce an alternative economic and financial architecture or security order (two of its newer members are at war with each other)
insights.locator: Paragraph on anti-Western screeds

insights.claim: Kotkin closes by framing four mutually exclusive scenarios for the future — a violent/authoritarian pre-modern multipolar order, a failed non-aligned movement recapture, a Global South utopia that mainly serves China's instrumental interests, or a reinvented, decolonised US-led Western order strengthened by middle-power agency — and endorses the fourth as the only option that actually exists and can be plausibly strengthened.
insights.speaker: Stephen Kotkin
insights.so_what: The essay's closing synthesis and clearest statement of Kotkin's own positioning — useful as a one-line summary framework for the whole piece's argument.
insights.quote: The reinvention of a decolonised US-led Western order, an option that suffers from an imperial past, hypocrisy and blundering
insights.locator: Final numbered list of four options
